## Findings by module

### 5

- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Arnheim's case for cuts and time jumps: film is 'partly' an illusion, so a jump in place or time (a door, then the maid inside) is accepted as 'turning a page'; a clean time continuum is needed inside a scene, but not between scenes. Gives the course a principled reason for its cut rules. Strongest single piece for the editing module from this book.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim's classification of montage, useful as a checklist for the course's editing section: (a) cutting unit length (long strips for quiet, short for tumult, mixed for shock); (b) whole scenes sequential, interlaced (crosscut) or inserted; (c) within a scene, long shot then details, details then long shot, or details only; (d) time relations (synchronism, before/after, neutral); (e) space relations; (f) subject links (similar shape, contrast of shape, similar or contrasting meaning). Arnheim's own note: good montage makes shots take on meaning from their neighbours.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim on telling without words, as a craft point for the course's sound and visual-storytelling sections: a gunshot shown by birds rising, a crowd's rhythm shown by heads swaying to unheard music (Les Nouveaux Messieurs). The visual equivalent carries the quality of the sound (sudden, rhythmic), so the audience sees the sound's character. Strong argument for planning shots that carry the audio's meaning.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim's summary of formative means (for a checklist): every object from one viewpoint; objects concealed behind or beside others; apparent size; light and shade with no colour; framing as selection; distance as a choice; time and space gaps by montage; spatial orientation relative; depth reduced; silence turned into the visible; camera movement as subjective state; reverse, accelerated and slow motion; stills; fades and dissolves as marks of a break; superimposition; special lenses; focus used as attention; mirror images. Use as the course's reference list of what the medium can do.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Arnheim on showing inner state through visible action, useful for directing and coverage: Suzanne's spilt tea (The Trial of the Count) shows suppressed feeling; a cigarette lit then held back shows change of heart (Flesh and the Devil). He says an actor 'acts' less in film, and that objects can carry feeling as well as faces. Good for the course's coverage notes on giving the camera a detail to carry the scene.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt): Motion and speed, Arnheim's craft points: close-ups make movement look faster, so actors act slower up close; a steep or oblique angle foreshortens travel and raises apparent speed; shorter shots look faster; balancing opposite directions across a cut keeps the eye at ease. Strong for the course's movement and pacing sections.
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Arnheim's thesis as he states it: photography and film are art because of what they lack compared with reality (depth, colour, full scale, sound), and those limits are the medium's material. The course can cite this for its 'limits as tools' theme. Arnheim is a theorist of 1933; treat his predictions about colour and wide screen as historical.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Camera-movement relativity in Arnheim: a pan or a camera that rolls is read as the objects moving unless the frame shows the camera's own body or a stable reference. A shot down on a bed looks like an upright man because the screen is read as vertical. Use as the reason to show a reference in moving and overhead shots.
- **note** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim's stroboscopic point: a cut of a few frames inside one continuous movement changes the action without the viewer noticing a cut (the 'imperceptible montage' of a man picked out of his stride). The stone lion in Potemkin is three statues. Useful for the course's 'cuts you don't see' note.
- **note** (ch-005.txt): Arnheim's visual analogy: a boot dinner in The Gold Rush (boot as fish, nails as bones, laces as spaghetti) carries the contrast of rich and poor through shape alone. A strong example for the course's 'shape as meaning' note (also in 'composition').
- **note** (ch-005.txt): Arnheim's test for a symbolic image: it must fit the world of the film. A tractor crashing fences (The General Line) is a symbol dragged in; a bureaucrat cleaning his pen on Lenin's head is motivated by the action. The same test applies to the fat woman seen from a window (A Woman of Paris): too obviously added. Use as the course's rule when a shot is meant to 'mean' something.
- **note** (ch-006.txt): Arnheim's argument against the 'complete' film (colour, wide screen, 3D): once the illusion is full, montage and camera moves feel like displacement and the film turns back into a stage recording. A view from 1933, contested later by filmmakers who used the wide screen and colour. Cite as one side of a debate, not as a forecast.
- **note** (ch-010.txt): Arnheim on sound in 1933-38: dialogue narrows the film to the human figure and paralyses the visual action (mouth movements are dead to the image); a film dialogue should be complete, not patchy. The argument is historical; the course can use it for its 'sound and picture' module as a statement of the 1930s case, with the later counter-arguments (Murch's sound-first editing) beside it.

### 3

- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Arnheim on what a lens and frame do to the picture: a single shot loses true depth and perspective (near objects look huge, a near table top looks trapezoidal), and the eye's constancy of size and shape do not fully work on screen. Shot distance sets the range of view, and projection size changes how fast motion looks. Good for the course's lens and screen-size sections.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim's angle-as-meaning examples: a camera placed behind the bars of a gate (Room's The Ghost That Never Returns) brings the prison into a shot that never shows it; a high angle turns a rowing boat into a form; a low angle makes an authority figure a mountain. The principle: a shot must show the object and its meaning, and the choice of angle is a choice of what to hide. Best source in this book for the course's camera-angle section.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim on the close-up and the long shot as a pair: a close-up can show a detail that stands for the whole (a fat man mopping his brow for a crowd), but too many close-ups lose the room and the people's positions, so pair them with long shots. Ways to go from detail to whole: cut, zoom or track back, or a mask that opens. Good for the course's shot-size section.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Arnheim notes that the stereoscopic film needs two images and special glasses for a group, and that film depth is 'between' flat and solid. Accurate for its period; 3D is now routine, so cite as history.
- **note** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim warns against angles chosen only for their look (Dreyer's Joan of Arc, a camera that roams the faces of a debate). Use as a caution in the course's angle and move sections: every shot must contribute to the action.
- **note** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim's size-change examples (a huge statue dwarfing two peasants, a staircase that grows as a boy climbs in The Crowd) show that perspective size, not real size, carries emotion when depth is flattened. Useful for the course's lens and staging sections.
- **note** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim's 'long shot' is defined by what is relevant to the situation, not by a fixed distance: a corner of a room that holds the hidden man (Keaton in The Cameraman) makes the shot a detail shot. Use as the course's own definition of shot size.

### 4

- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim on light as form: the cameraman decides how each object reads by placing lamps and shadows; the same face can be bony and vivid or flat and grey (Pudovkin's Baranovskaya vs a German studio), and a single bright beam across a dark room is a black-and-white effect colour cannot match. Strong for the course's lighting-as-storytelling module, with its 1933 date stated.

### 6

- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Arnheim's note on capture rate: the faster the subject moves, the shorter each exposure must be and the shorter the gap between frames if the phases are to be caught; Marey's 12-per-second rifle could not catch bird flight. Use as the historical reason behind the course's shutter and frame-rate rules. Also: motion is relative to the camera's station point (Promio's travelling shot in Venice).
- **note** (ch-004.txt): Arnheim's speed notes, dated but workable: accelerated motion shows speed (Eisenstein's office scene), slow motion makes movement look like a new 'original', and frame-cutting inside a movement changes it. Use as the origin of the high-speed effect; the course's exposure arithmetic is in the other sources.
- **note** (ch-007.txt): Arnheim's mechanics of intermittent motion: a claw pulls the film frame by frame, a Maltese cross advances it, and a shutter covers the gate while it moves. Film is one continuous record, split into frames for capture and projection. Good background for the course's shutter and movement notes.
